# What this queue actually RAN, by digest.
#
# GENERATED — do not edit by hand. Refresh with:
#     npm run migrations:digests
# which reads `public.schema_migration_queue` through Mission Control's
# `/hooks/migration-enqueue` `digests` action. `apply-migrations.yml` verifies
# this file against the live queue on every migration push, so a hand-edited or
# stale entry is caught there rather than believed here.
#
# ## What it is for
#
# `schema_migration_queue.sha256` has been written since the first version of
# this queue, and its own comment says it exists "so what RAN can be compared
# to the repo". Nothing ever compared it. Measured 12 Sep 2026: 2 of 55 settled
# rows already differed from their repository file, and no surface anywhere
# said so.
#
# Editing a migration that has already applied is the mistake the pipeline
# refuses everywhere else — `enqueue` will not overwrite the SQL of a version
# it holds, and the apply workflow prints a warning for a modified file. But
# that warning fires only for the push that does it, and only if the push went
# through that workflow. Nothing checked afterwards, and nothing checked a file
# edited by any other route. This is that check.
#
# ## What a mismatch means
#
# The repository's copy of a migration no longer matches the SQL that ran. The
# database is unaffected — it already ran what it ran — so this is never an
# emergency. What is lost is the repository's claim to describe the schema:
# anyone reading the file, or replaying the corpus anywhere, gets something
# other than what happened here.
#
# The remedy is NEVER to rewrite the queue's copy, which is history. Put the
# file back, or carry the change in a new migration.
#
# Format: <version>  <sha256 of the SQL that ran>  <filename as submitted>
